aiItems.content:
What is a cherry blossom painting?

A cherry blossom painting is a piece of artwork that depicts the flowering branches of the cherry blossom tree — known in Japan as sakura — and is one of the most enduring motifs in Asian art and culture. These paintings traditionally use ink wash or watercolour techniques to capture the delicate, fleeting beauty of blossom blooms, often set against soft or minimal backgrounds in keeping with Japanese artistic values. In contemporary home decor, cherry blossom paintings are popular for their calming, nature-inspired quality and their versatility — they suit Japandi, minimalist and Asian-inspired interiors especially well. A set of wall art prints featuring cherry blossom scenes is a simple, impactful way to bring that sense of quiet beauty into a bedroom or living space.

How to Hang a Cherry Blossom Painting Set of 3 in a Bedroom

1. Choose your wall: Pick a wall with enough horizontal space for all three prints side by side — above the bed's headboard is the most popular spot, as it creates a natural focal point in the room.

2. Measure and mark: Lay the three prints on the floor first to work out your preferred spacing — a gap of 5 to 8 cm between each print usually looks balanced. Mark the hanging points on the wall with a pencil before putting in any fixings.

3. Hang at eye level: The centre of the prints should sit roughly at eye level when you're standing — for most bedrooms that's around 145 to 155 cm from the floor to the middle of each print. If hanging above a headboard, aim for the bottom of the prints to sit about 15 to 20 cm above the top of the headboard.

4. Check alignment: Use a spirit level across all three prints once they're up — even a slight tilt is really noticeable with a set. Step back and look from the doorway to get the full effect.

5. Style around the prints: Keep the surrounding decor simple to let the Japandi ink artwork breathe — natural textures, neutral bedding and minimal clutter on bedside tables will let the set do the work.

Choosing Your Cherry Blossom Wall Art Print Format

Unframed Print — The print only, ready for you to frame in your own choice of frame. Available on Luster art paper (vibrant, semi-sheen finish) or Museum quality paper (ultra-fine detail, archival standard). Great if you already have a frame or want to match your own decor exactly.

Framed Print — Your chosen print is mounted and framed, arriving completely ready to hang — no sourcing a frame, no hassle. Available in multiple sizes on Luster or Museum quality paper. The most convenient option if you want the set on your wall with minimal effort.

Wrapped Canvas — The artwork is printed directly onto canvas and wrapped around a wooden stretcher frame — no glazing, no frame needed. Has a natural texture that suits the ink-brush style of this Japandi set particularly well. Simply hang straight onto the wall. Available in a range of canvas sizes.

Paper quality: Luster vs Museum — Luster art paper gives a semi-gloss, vibrant finish that makes the black ink and red blossom tones pop. Museum quality paper is the premium archival choice — it captures every fine detail in the brushwork and is made to last for decades without fading. Both are printed with fade-resistant pigment inks in the UK.

Line art is a style of illustration that uses distinct, clean lines drawn against a plain background — most commonly black on white — with no shading, gradients or filled colour areas. This simplicity is exactly what gives line art its modern, minimalist appeal, making it a popular choice for contemporary home décor. Vintage posters are art prints designed in the style of classic, retro or historical imagery — drawing on the visual language of past decades to create a timeless, characterful look on your wall. They can feature anything from classic cars, travel destinations and old advertising to botanical illustrations and black and white photography, all rendered with a nostalgic quality that feels both familiar and stylish. In home decor, vintage posters are popular because they work across a huge range of interior styles — from industrial and masculine bedrooms to eclectic living spaces — and they bring personality and a sense of history to a room instantly. Sets of three are especially popular, as they allow you to create a cohesive gallery wall with a single purchase.

How to Hang Vintage Posters as a Set of 3 in a Bedroom

1. Choose your wall: Pick a wall with enough width to display all three prints side by side comfortably — above a bed headboard or along a main feature wall are the most popular spots for a set of three.

3. Find your centre point: Measure the total width of all three prints plus your chosen gaps, then find the centre of that measurement and line it up with the centre of your wall or bed. This keeps the set looking balanced and intentional.

4. Mark your hanging points: Use a pencil and a spirit level to mark where each hook or nail will go before you commit. Getting the horizontal line right across all three prints is the most important step for a professional result.

Prints for living room are wall art prints designed specifically to suit the scale, style and colour palettes most commonly found in living spaces. Good living room prints reflect the mood you want to create, whether that's calm and nature-inspired, bold and graphic, or soft and decorative. How to Hang Prints for Living Room Walls the Easy Way

1. Measure your wall space first: Before you order, measure the width of the wall or furniture piece you're hanging above (e.g. your sofa). As a general guide, your set of prints should span roughly two-thirds of the width of the sofa or sideboard beneath them for the most balanced look.

2. Choose your layout: For a set of 3 prints, a horizontal row at eye level is the most popular arrangement — aim for gaps of 5–8 cm between each print. Alternatively, a vertical stack works well in a narrow alcove or tall wall space.

How to Hang and Arrange Paintings for Home Office

1. Choose your wall: Pick the wall you look at most while working — above your desk or directly in your eyeline is ideal. This makes the art part of your working environment rather than something you forget is there.

2. Plan your layout before you hang: Lay the three prints on the floor first and step back to check the spacing. For a set of 3, an even gap of around 5–8 cm between each print looks clean and intentional. Use a spirit level or a length of masking tape along the wall to keep the tops aligned.

3. Hang at eye level: The centre of the prints should sit roughly at eye level when you're seated at your desk — that's usually around 120–130 cm from the floor. It feels much more natural than hanging art at standing height in a room where you spend most of your time sitting.

4. Step back and adjust: Once they're up, sit at your desk and look at them from your working position. Small shifts left or right are easy at this stage. If you've chosen the framed option, it arrives ready to hang so there's no extra effort needed.
